prompt:
Patient is a 39-year-old woman who lives alone with 2 cats in a suburban apartment, with a history of chronic pain disorder who presents with 4 weeks of involuntary, jerking movements of the torso and all four extremities. They occur at rest and she has never experienced this before. There is no clear trigger with activity or pain. She notes that she did a weeklong trial of naltrexone prior to the onset of these movements, which she stopped. She does not engage in substance use and has not been on opioids. Neurologic examination and routine laboratory studies (CBC, basic metabolic panel, and liver enzymes) are normal, however the movements persist and interfere with her ability to sleep and function. What are the next steps for evaluating the cause? What can be done to manage her abnormal movements?

Provide a comprehensive management plan including appropriate diagnostic workup, referrals, procedures if indicated, follow-up, and actions to avoid.

rubric_items.text: Refer the patient to a movement-disorders neurologist for prompt evaluation.
Characterize the movements through a detailed neurologic examination assessing distribution, rhythm, stimulus sensitivity, suppressibility, distractibility, and entrainment.
Obtain video documentation of representative movements during the examination or from a smartphone recording.
Perform a comprehensive review of prescription drugs, over-the-counter medications, and supplements for movement-inducing agents.
Obtain a detailed exposure history covering toxins, travel, infections, and animal contacts.
Obtain a detailed family history of movement disorders, seizures, psychiatric disease, and early neurologic illness.
Counsel the patient to avoid further naltrexone exposure because of the temporal association with symptom onset.
Obtain brain MRI for persistent unexplained new-onset movements; add intravenous contrast when clinical or imaging findings warrant it.
Obtain video EEG monitoring to determine whether the movements have an epileptic correlate.
Perform surface EMG polymyography with EEG cortical back-averaging to classify persistent diagnostically unclear myoclonus.
Obtain a metabolic evaluation including calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, renal and hepatic indices, vitamin B12, and folate.
Measure TSH and free T4.
Obtain Wilson disease testing (ceruloplasmin and 24-hour urinary copper) when movement phenomenology or associated hepatic, psychiatric, ocular, or family-history findings raise clinical suspicion.
Arrange a slit-lamp examination for Kayser-Fleischer rings if Wilson disease is clinically suspected.
Obtain a urine toxicology screen for unreported or inadvertent drug exposure.
Order infectious testing (e.g., HIV, syphilis) when supported by the history, examination, or epidemiology; reserve Lyme serology for a compatible clinical syndrome with plausible exposure.
Use rheumatologic serology when clinical findings suggest systemic autoimmune disease; order ANA first and add ENA or anti-dsDNA when supported by the ANA result and clinical suspicion.
Assess for positive examination features of a functional movement disorder rather than diagnosing it solely by exclusion.
Explain the possibility and nature of a functional movement disorder in a validating, nonjudgmental manner.
Refer for physical therapy specializing in functional neurologic disorder rehabilitation when functional features are identified.
Use a short course of low-dose clonazepam for symptomatic relief while the diagnostic evaluation proceeds.
Arrange neurology follow-up within 2 to 4 weeks to review testing and reassess the movements.
Counsel the patient to avoid driving, heights, swimming alone, and heavy machinery while the movements remain uncontrolled.
Provide emergency-return precautions for altered awareness, new weakness, fever, rapidly worsening movements, or injury.
Reassure the patient that the normal initial examination and laboratory studies do not indicate an immediate life-threatening process.
Restart or continue naltrexone despite its temporal association with the new movements.
Use dopamine-blocking agents such as haloperidol, metoclopramide, or prochlorperazine to suppress the movements empirically.
Start chronic high-dose or long-term benzodiazepine therapy without specialist supervision.
Empirically prescribe levodopa-carbidopa for presumed parkinsonism.
Initiate tetrabenazine before establishing the movement phenomenology and diagnosis.
Prescribe opioid analgesics to control the movements or associated chronic pain.
Diagnose conversion disorder and refer only to psychiatry without a neurologic evaluation.
Reassure the patient that no additional evaluation or follow-up is necessary.
Initiate antiseizure medication solely because of nonspecific EEG findings without electroclinical evidence of seizures.
Empirically treat toxoplasmosis based only on cat ownership.
Advise unrestricted driving, swimming alone, or operation of heavy machinery while the movements are uncontrolled.
Initiate empiric high-dose systemic corticosteroids without evidence supporting autoimmune or inflammatory disease.
Begin penicillamine or trientine chelation for presumed Wilson disease before confirming the diagnosis.
Order whole-body PET-CT for indiscriminate malignancy or paraneoplastic screening.
Diagnose the movements as opioid withdrawal despite the absence of opioid exposure.
